title: POC Weekly Check-in — TTFT & Kernel Tuning
summary: Weekly POC sync to review last week's benchmark results focusing on TTFT and streaming, discuss kernel choices for int8/quantized runtimes, and plan next tuning steps. Customer reported inconsistent TTFT regressions when switching to 4-bit kernels; SE proposed hybrid kernel routing and prefix caching changes. Agreed to run two focused experiments: 1) streaming warmup with short prefix cache priming, 2) split-merge kernel route (fast start low-fidelity kernel then switch to high-fidelity) on Dedicated pool. Next meeting booked after benchmark run. Security docs link and perf spreadsheet shared.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42m
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Leah Chen (Redwood SE), Mark Hollis (Aurelia Head of ML), Priya Rao (Aurelia Platform), Diego Fuentes (Aurelia SRE)
Shared links: perf spreadsheet: https://redwood-sharing.example/pocttft2025, security packet: https://redwood.example/security/aur-msa.pdf

Summary/Topics (auto): TTFT regressions on quant kernels; streaming latency; sequence length distribution; KV cache priming; kernel routing strategies.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick 30 minute run through then open q and a — Leah and I will cover the tuning notes, Mark/Diego feel free to jump in with logs.
[00:22] Mark: yep thanks Samir, sorry running a bit late, had an incident with the staging deploy, mostly resolved now.
[00:30] Leah: cool, let's kick off with the headline numbers from last week's bench — i pulled the spreadsheet into the call, but short version: baseline TTFT median on hosted was ~120ms, on Dedicated using int8 kernels we saw a median of 210ms and a heavy tail to 800ms on some long-context prompts.
[00:52] Priya: just to clarify, baseline is previous float16 kernel on Dedicated?
[00:58] Leah: baseline is our float16 optimized kernel on our standard host SKU - that had good TTFT because it uses the fast attention kernel for small seqs. Dedicated int8 moved to a quantized kernel path that benefits tokens/sec later but its first-token path is slower sometimes because of extra dequant steps and alternate kernel scheduling.
[01:20] Diego: we noticed the spikes are correlated with cold KV cache, like when the same long prefix hasn't been requested for a while.
[01:30] Samir: yep that matches our hypothesis — KV cache and prefix reuse plays a big role. two immediate levers: 1) priming the cache on service start or on request path, 2) hybrid kernel routing: use a low-latency kernel for the first N tokens then switch to the quant kernel for subsequent generation.
[01:55] Mark: i like hybrid, but curious about complexity and correctness — does kernel switching cause any output divergence?
[02:05] Leah: good question — if you switch after a token boundary and retain the same KV cache semantics, the logits should be consistent in theory, but in practice numerical differences in quantized vs fp16 can change probabilities slightly. we've done internal experiments where switching at token 1 had <0.5% quality delta on our eval set.
[02:33] Priya: that might be acceptable — our product PM set a hard TTFT requirement of 200ms 95p but can tolerate minor token-level variance if semantics aren't totally broken.
[02:47] Diego: what about streaming? some of our user journeys rely on partial tokens streaming quickly — switching kernel mid-stream could disrupt streaming frame pacing.
[02:58] Leah: right, streaming adds two constraints: you need to emit first chunk fast and preserve steady-state throughput. our proposal: emit first-token/first-chunk using the fast-start kernel (lower context optimizer), then asynchronously warm the quant kernel, swapping once it's warmed and KV primed. the client sees continuous streaming but under the hood we transition.
[03:20] Mark: any memory overhead when maintaining two kernel paths?
[03:25] Leah: negligible if you schedule the warmup only for requests that hit the hybrid route; the runtime keeps both kernel codepaths resident but memory overhead is small compared to model weights. the main cost is the extra warmup compute which looks like 1-2 extra forward passes per request for warmup priming — that's why batching and burst capacity matter.
[03:48] Samir: and that's where Dedicated burst capacity helps — you can reserve a small burst pool for these warmups so tail latency doesn't hit the production pool. i'll follow up with a delta price for 100 concurrent warmup slots.
[04:02] Diego: okay can you also include burst autoscale rules? we don't want extra cost surprises.
[04:08] Samir: yes.
[04:10] Leah: next i want to walk through the sequence length distribution you sent, Mark — looks like 60% of requests are <128 tokens, 30% 128-512, and 10% >512. that skew is good for TTFT tuning because most requests are short. if we bias the fast-start kernel for <128 it'll cover majority.
[04:34] Mark: that's accurate, though our critical user path tends to have 400-600 token prompts for records fetches — those are most sensitive to tail latency.
[04:42] Leah: for those, priming the KV with the record retrieval prefix helps a lot. i pushed a small priming script to your test endpoint earlier this morning, it sends the common prefixes immediately after deploy to seed the cache.
[04:57] Priya: i saw the job in our test infra, it ran once but maybe didn't cover all prefixes. can we schedule it to run on a cron or on-demand via webhook?
[05:05] Leah: yes we can do cron or trigger on first request detection. for the POC we'll do a scheduled priming before bench runs so numbers are reproducible.
[05:14] Diego: about kernel choices, what's the gap between 4-bit and 8-bit int quant in your tests?
[05:21] Leah: 4-bit (gptq-like) gives best token/sec, but TTFT variability increases because the kernel path is more specialized and sometimes requires extra dequantization overhead. 8-bit sits in the middle. float16 still has the best TTFT but worse cost. so it's a cost/latency/quality tradeoff.
[05:43] Mark: and did you run the split-kernel where first 1-4 tokens use fp16 then switch?
[05:48] Leah: yes we ran a micro-experiment — split at token 1 reduced median TTFT by ~75ms on long-context cases, but gave a small quality delta. we put the exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[06:00] Samir: i will call out the spreadsheet location again: https://redwood-sharing.example/pocttft2025 — there's a 'hybrid' tab and raw traces.
[06:10] Mark: okay opening it now.
[06:20] [screen shuffle/noise]
[06:30] Priya: one more platform ask: can we get the first-byte latency histogram rather than tokenized steps? our telemetry currently measures request start to first-byte, not token boundary.
[06:43] Leah: yes the runtime emits both metrics, we can wire a dashboard for first-byte and first-token; sometimes first-byte is faster because it includes header/stream overhead.
[06:53] Diego: we also saw occasional streaming stalls around token 80-120 in long gens — is that a batching issue?
[07:01] Leah: likely batching + cache eviction. When the queue mixes long and short seqs, the scheduler tries to pack but sometimes the KV cache for that long session hasn't warmed, causing slight stalls as kernel loads different codepaths. We have two mitigations: mispredictive packing avoidance (force separate lanes for long sessions) and proactive cache priming.
[07:24] Mark: is there an easy flag we can toggle to separate long versus short lanes?
[07:29] Leah: yes, we can set a per-route inference policy: max_batch_for_short=32, and route >512 to a long-lane with separate pool. we'll add config sample to the shared doc.
[07:40] Samir: also note you can pin model variant for route, so your records-fetch route can use float16 pinned, while conversational uses quantized.
[07:50] Priya: that sounds promising. is it supported on Private (VPC) as well?
[07:55] Leah: yes same control plane for Hosted/Dedicated/Private. kernel scheduling is runtime-level so Private installs will get same options, assuming you have the runtime version with hybrid-kernel.
[08:07] Diego: question about reproducibility — our perf runs showed different tails each run. how do we make bench runs deterministic?
[08:15] Leah: a few tips: 1) ensure priming step runs before measurement, 2) use fixed concurrency patterns rather than open-loop ramp, 3) pin routing/pool IDs, and 4) disable autoscale during the test window. we put a bench-run recipe in the spreadsheet.
[08:33] Mark: we tried disabling autoscale but didn't pin pool ids — i think that caused cross-traffic.
[08:38] Samir: ok we'll include the concrete runbook steps in the email.
[08:42] Priya: any security notes from changing kernels? like attestation or KMS implications?
[08:48] Leah: no KMS change; kernels are runtime binaries we manage in Redwood images. for Private there's an option to run only signed kernels and we can provide hashes for attestation. no key material moves.
[09:03] Diego: good. also curious if quant kernels affect auditing/tracing? our APM tags come out different sometimes.
[09:10] Leah: traces include kernel tag now in our runtime 2.3 release; we'll surface that so you can filter by kernel type.
[09:18] Mark: can you remind us the impact on cost if we run hybrid for say 50% of traffic?
[09:24] Samir: rough back-of-envelope: hybrid increases compute by ~5-12% due to warmups depending on split point, but reduces long-tail TTFT which reduces perceived SLA violations. i will include a modeled spreadsheet showing cost at 25/50/75% hybrid adoption.
[09:42] Priya: ok would like to see that.
[09:45] [pause / typing sounds]
[10:00] Leah: quick demo of a short run I captured earlier — i'll read out a trimmed trace: Request A (seq 64) baseline fp16 TTFT 110ms, quant int8 TTFT 190ms, hybrid-first-token fp16->int8 TTFT 125ms. Long prompt B (seq 520) baseline fp16 TTFT 220ms, quant int8 TTFT 420ms, hybrid TTFT 260ms.
[10:34] Mark: that's compelling. where's the quality eval?
[10:36] Leah: there's a tiny quality delta in log-prob alignment — we measured perplexity and 99p overlap on our prompt sample, numbers are in the 'quality' tab. overall overlap >98% for hybrid.
[10:49] Diego: for the benchmarking runs you mentioned earlier, do they include streaming chunk size tuning? we found chunk size of 64 bytes vs 256 changes first-chunk emission.
[10:58] Leah: yes tuning chunk size is part of the bench matrix; smaller initial chunk helps single-byte-first scenarios but can increase overhead. we'll include chunk-size as a variable in the next run.
[11:11] Samir: okay timeline — Leah proposed two experiments: A) KV-priming scheduled batch, B) Hybrid kernel enabled for short route. each run 3x and capture TTFT median and 95p.
[11:23] Leah: experiment details: run A with priming job run 5 minutes before bench, concurrency 40, fixed seed traffic replay. Run B with hybrid enabled for routes <128 tokens and a switch point at token 4. We'll also include chunk size sweep 64/128/256.
[11:42] Mark: and where will the traces land?
[11:45] Leah: I'll push raw traces to the spreadsheet link and also provide a link to a GCS bucket with full logs.
[11:53] Samir: action items we'll capture in the follow up email. can we get Diego to run the priming cron in your test infra?
[11:59] Diego: yes will run and report.
[12:02] Priya: one more ask: can we have an endpoint that simulates cold-start after 30 minutes idle? we want to see user-facing worst-case.
[12:10] Leah: yes we have a 'cold-sim' flag that flushes KV and then runs a sample; we'll include that in the bench recipe.
[12:19] Mark: great. supplier/competitor question — any reason we'd consider Anthropic models for this workload? they sometimes have different latency characteristics.
[12:28] Samir: Anthropic can give good quality and predictable RT but cost and hosting flexibility vary; we can include a competitor comparison if you want.
[12:36] Priya: please do.
[12:40] [brief silence]
[12:55] Samir: ok last bit — scheduling: can we aim to have initial runs done by EoD 2025-04-18?
[13:03] Mark: yes we can aim for that but will confirm once Diego sets up cron.
[13:08] Samir: perfect. quick recap?
[13:11] Mark: recap comfortable?
[13:13] Samir: recap — Leah to run priming script and hybrid route in test, customer to provide prompt sets and runbench per recipe, Redwood to share cost model and traces. Follow-up 2025-04-22 to review.
[13:28] Priya: sounds good.
[13:32] Diego: thanks all.

[13:38] Mark: none from me.
